newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Stals snuffs out lingering S.Africa rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: Stals snuffs out lingering S.Africa rate cut hopes.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals on Friday snuffed out any lingering hopes of a near-term cut in South African interest rates, warning the next move could in fact be up.
Economists said the central bank head had fired a warning shot across the markets' bows, cautioning that expectations of a significant cut in interest rates this year were ill-founded.

"I don't actually think it means there will be a rate hike but it definitely does dim the hope of getting a rate cut later this year, as many analysts have been expecting," said Anastasia Gekis, economist with ABN AMRO in Johannesburg.
Stals told a conference in Durban that even more stringent measures might be needed to curb liquidity and excessive credit growth, leading to even higher interest rates.
"Recent trends in the money supply and bank credit extension beg the question...whether monetary policy at this juncture is restrictive enough," he said.
The news shocked the market, sending bond yields 10 basis points higher at one stage, as both local and foreign investors dumped stock.

Bond traders said Stals' comments might mean that March money supply and private credit figures due at 1500 GMT would be worse than expected. But some analysts said Stals would not have received March figures at the time of preparing his speech.

Economists predict a consensus 16.50 percent increase in March private sector credit extension growth compared with a preliminary 17.34 percent rise in February. M3 money supply growth is expected to show a 15.04 pecent year-on-year rise from February's preliminary 15.82 percent.

Henry Flint, economist at Mathison and Hollidge, noted Stals earlier this week cautioned it was premature to suggest a lower money market shortage signalled an end to the liquidity squeeze. Now he was underlining the point by demanding evidence of a sustained slowdown in money supply and credit growth.
"I think Stals wants to get the message across that he wants to see a sustained decline in monetary aggregates to reasonable levels," Flint said.
The central bank's target for M3 growth in 1997 is six to ten percent.
Back in January, many analysts had been looking for two or three one percentage point interest rate cuts during 1997.

But more recently expectations have been toned down with two leading economists -- Dave Mohr of Old Mutual and Edward Osborn of Edey Rogers -- suggesting this week that there may be no move this year, despite clear signals of spending growth tailing off.

In addition to excess money and credit growth, the Reserve Bank would be reluctant to ease ahead of measures to relax exchange controls on individuals from July 1, which would require high interest rates to discourage an exodus of local capital, Mohr said.
At the same time, the recent increase in U.S. rates had reduced the room for manouevre further.
South Africa's official Bank rate currently stands at 17.0 percent, following a one point hike last November, while commercial banks' prime lending rate is 20.25 percent.
Stals reiterated in Durban his determination to bear down on inflation in order to provide financial stability for economic growth.
But his approach was strongly criticised by Chris Edwards of the Overseas Development Group at Britain's University of East Anglia, speaking at the same conference.

He argued the Reserve Bank was pursuing deflationary policies more suited to a developed European economy which would not deal with South Africa's chronic unemployment problem, afflicting one third of the workforce.

"The Reserve Bank needs to be brought under much tighter parliamentary control and must be restructured so as not be dominated by representatives of big business. If that means sacking Chris Stals then so be it," Edwards said.
